introduction-code-is-law.core: Code decides what people can and cannot do: who sees data, whether it can be deleted, which choices are easy. Engineers are de facto regulators and share responsibility for those outcomes.

first_principles.problem: Engineers treat ethics as someone else's job (legal, product), yet they write the if-statements and schemas that enforce or violate users' rights.
truths: Implementers have power to raise concerns.
derivation: Recognise that **design choices are policy**.
Ask **who is affected and how** by each feature.
Raise concerns early, through **process**, not heroics.

analogy.title: An architect placing doors
analogy.story: Where the doors go decides how people move through a building, and whether wheelchair users can enter at all.
analogy.breaks: Buildings get inspected against codes. Software ethics rarely does, so engineers must apply their own standards.

example.title: A data-retention default
example.scenario: Logs keep full user data forever by default.

steps.label: Power
steps.detail: An engineer's default affects every user.

example.outcome: engineers see their choices as policy decisions.

check.a: Their code decides what users can and cannot do, at scale.

privacy-by-design-gdprccpa.core: Privacy by design (GDPR Article 25) builds data protection into architecture from the start: collect the minimum, limit purpose and retention, protect by default, and make deletion and access possible.

first_principles.problem: Treating privacy as a cookie banner leaves systems that hoard personal data everywhere, can't delete it, and fail audits or leak in breaches.
truths: Data you don't collect can't leak.
Personal data spreads into logs, backups and analytics.
Users have legal rights to access and deletion.
derivation: **Minimise**: collect only what's needed.
**Purpose-limit** and **retention-limit** data.
**Protect by default**: encryption, access control, pseudonymisation.
Design for **subject rights**: export and delete across all stores.

analogy.title: Fire safety in building design
analogy.story: Sprinklers and exits are designed in from the blueprint, not added after the first fire.
analogy.breaks: Fire codes are inspected at build time. Privacy compliance is ongoing as data flows change.

example.title: Right to be forgotten
flow: Data in DB, logs, analytics, backups

steps.label: Design fix
steps.detail: Use user IDs, not emails, in logs so deletion is tractable.

example.outcome: deletion requests are a routine job, not a crisis.

check.a: Collecting and keeping only the personal data needed for a specific purpose.

dark-patterns-in-ux.core: Dark patterns are interfaces deliberately designed to trick users: hidden costs, roach-motel cancellation, confirmshaming, pre-ticked boxes. Engineers implement them and can refuse or push back.

first_principles.problem: Conversion and retention metrics reward manipulation, so teams ship designs that trap users, damaging trust and increasingly breaking laws.
truths: It erodes trust and invites regulation.
derivation: Learn to **recognise** patterns (roach motel, sneak into basket, confirmshaming, disguised ads).
Apply a **symmetry test**: is cancelling as easy as signing up?
Push for **long-term metrics** (retention via value, complaints).
Escalate through **ethics review** processes.

analogy.title: A shop with no visible exit
analogy.story: Easy to walk in, maze-like to leave. You may buy something, but you won't return.
analogy.breaks: Shops are regulated physically. Software dark patterns are increasingly regulated (FTC, EU DSA), but enforcement lags.

branches.label: Tests
children: Would you explain it to users?

example.title: Cancellation flow
example.scenario: Product asks for a 6-step cancellation with guilt messages.

steps.label: Alternative
steps.detail: A short exit survey gives real retention data instead.

example.outcome: users leave cleanly and the team learns why.

check.a: Easy to get into (sign up) but hard to get out of (cancel).

accessibility-as-an-ethical-imperative.core: Accessibility lets people with visual, auditory, motor and cognitive disabilities use your software. It's often a legal requirement, and like curb cuts, it improves usability for everyone.

first_principles.problem: Inaccessible apps exclude millions of users, attract thousands of lawsuits a year, and are expensive to retrofit.
truths: Many users have disabilities, permanent or temporary.
Accessibility laws apply to most software.
derivation: Follow **WCAG** (semantic HTML, contrast, keyboard navigation, alt text, captions).
Test with **automated tools** and **screen readers**.
Include accessibility in **definition of done** and CI.

analogy.title: Curb cuts
analogy.story: Ramps cut into pavements for wheelchairs also help prams, cyclists and travellers with suitcases.
analogy.breaks: Curb cuts are visible. Software barriers are invisible to those who don't need assistive tech.

example.title: An inaccessible checkout
example.scenario: Buttons are clickable divs with no labels.

steps.label: Prevention
steps.detail: Automated accessibility checks fail the build on regressions.

code.text: Pay

points: Test in CI and with assistive tech.

check.a: Features built for people with disabilities end up benefiting many other users too.

the-ethics-of-ai-automation.core: Algorithms encode human choices about what to optimise and which data to learn from. Automated decisions can scale bias, so build in data checks, fairness testing, explainability, human oversight and appeal paths.

first_principles.problem: "The algorithm decided" hides human decisions. A model trained on biased data quietly denies loans or jobs to whole groups at scale.
derivation: Audit **training data** for representation.
Test **outcomes across groups**.
Provide **explanations** for decisions.
Keep **humans in the loop** for high-stakes decisions.
Offer **appeals** and monitor drift.

analogy.title: A rubber stamp
analogy.story: Automating a biased clerk's decisions doesn't remove the bias; it stamps it on thousands of applications per minute.
analogy.breaks: A clerk can be questioned. Models need explicit explainability tooling.

example.title: Automated résumé screening
example.scenario: A model rejects candidates from certain schools disproportionately.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Proxy features (postcode, school) carried historical bias.

check.q: Why doesn't removing a protected attribute guarantee fairness?
check.a: Other features can act as proxies that correlate with it.

building-an-ethical-engineering-practice.core: Ethics works when it's built into process like security: checklists in design reviews, impact assessments, escalation paths and metrics, not reliance on one brave engineer.

first_principles.problem: Ethical problems get caught only when an individual happens to notice and speak up, which is unreliable and risky for that person.
derivation: Add **ethics questions** to design and PR templates.
Run **impact assessments** for features touching personal data or vulnerable users.
Create a **safe escalation path**.
Track **ethics metrics** (complaints, accessibility issues).

analogy.title: Security in the deployment pipeline
analogy.story: You don't rely on someone remembering to add authentication; the pipeline requires it. Ethics checks can work the same way.
analogy.breaks: Security failures are often binary. Ethical issues involve judgement, so checklists prompt discussion rather than auto-block.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Concerns are raised as normal review comments, not acts of courage.

check.a: So issues are caught routinely, rather than depending on one person noticing and taking a personal risk.
